description_full: Lasertec Corporation engages in the design, manufacture, and sale of inspection and measurement equipment in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Other Asia, the United States, and Europe. The company offers semiconductor related products, including Actinic EUV patterned mask inspection system, EUV mask blanks inspection and review system, mask inspection system, mask blanks inspection and review system, EUV pellicle inspection system, EUV mask backside inspection and cleaning system, and mask edge inspection system; phase-shift and transmittance measurement system, and phase-shift measurement system; SiC wafer inspection and review system, GaN wafer inspection and review system, high sensitivity under-layer defect inspection and review system, multi-wavelength wafer inspection system, high sensitivity wafer edge inspection system, wafer edge-dimension measurement system, via depth measurement system, TSV back grinding process measurement system, and automated wafer measurement system. It also provides FPD photomask inspection system, pellicle inspection and pellicle mounting system for CLIOS, and FPD mask blanks inspection system; and microscopes, such as laser microscopes, automatic inspection and review system, infrared confocal microscope, electro-chemical reaction visualizing confocal system, and in-situ observation at ultra-high temperature confocal scanning laser microscope. The company was formerly known as NJS Corporation and changed its name to Lasertec Corporation in 1986. Lasertec Corporation was founded in 1960 and is headquartered in Yokohama, Japan.

financial_summary: Lasertec Corp. is a large-cap technology business with a $20.6B market cap on $1.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 56% against a 10% cost of capital — a 46-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 57% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $293M in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.63×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
Accruals are elevated at +8.6% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.3%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 9.0% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
